mainTopic: בישולי גוים and other foods of גויים: which are permitted and which are forbidden
overview: This amud is about food that גויים cooked or prepared (בישולי גוים), and when it is still permitted. First the גמרא rules that food is forbidden only if a גוי did all of the cooking. If a Jew placed the food on the fire or turned it over, it is permitted, and רבינא applies this to bread, even when the Jew only stoked the coals. Next come disputes about salted fish and roasted eggs, and a story at the house of ריש גלותא where רב זביד rules like רבי יוחנן that a roasted egg is forbidden. A ברייתא lists simple foods of גויים that are permitted, and the גמרא explains what the bean called שיעתא is and how it was grown. Then come rules about date husks cooked in large or small pots, which depend on נותן טעם לפגם. רב ספרא challenges רב ששת's ban on cooked oil, and רבי אסי says boiled medium dates are forbidden. רב and לוי argue about the dish שתיתא, and in practice people were lenient. Finally, חזקיה and רבי יוחנן argue about benefiting from pickles of גויים that are known to contain wine. The answer to the last question comes on the next amud.

steps.title: A gentile woman may stir the Jewish woman's pot
steps.stepSummary: This is the end of a ruling that started just before. A גוי woman may stir a pot that a Jewish woman put on the fire until the Jewish woman comes back, and there is nothing to worry about.
steps.simpleTranslation: And she (the gentile woman) stirs it until she (the Jewish woman) comes back from the bathhouse or from the synagogue, and she need not worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling it began a moment ago: the Jewish woman put the pot on, and the גוי woman only stirs it while she is out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Jew started the cooking by placing the pot on the fire. The גוי only helps it along by stirring, even until it is finished. Because the Jew began the cooking, the food is not treated as בישולי גוים.

keyTerms.meaning: she need not worry; there is no concern

phrases.english: and she stirs it, until she comes back
phrases.notes: The גוי woman does the stirring. The Jewish woman, who put the pot on the fire, is the one coming back.

phrases.english: from the bathhouse or from the synagogue,
and she need not be concerned.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְגִיסָה, עַד שֶׁתָּבֹא מִבֵּית הַמֶּרְחָץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ruling that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a Jew put the pot on the fire, a גוי may stir it and finish it, and the food is permitted.

steps.title: What if the gentile placed it and the Jew turned it over?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask about the reverse case: the גוי put the meat on the fire, and the Jew only turned it over.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: if a gentile placed the meat on the fire and a Jew turned it over, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question, the opposite of the previous case. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous case the Jew started the cooking. Here the גוי started it, and the Jew only joined in partway. The question is whether the Jew's turning is enough to make the food permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: a question was asked among them (the חכמים)

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
if a gentile placed it and a Jew turned it over, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the case in step 1, asking about the reverse order of who did what.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether meat is permitted when a גוי put it on the fire but a Jew turned it over.

steps.title: A קל וחומר: if the Jew finished the cooking, surely it is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers with a קל וחומר. If the food is permitted when the גוי finished the cooking, it is certainly permitted when the Jew finished it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: it is a קל וחומר. If it is permitted when its finishing was done by a gentile, then when its finishing was done by a Jew, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the question from step 2 and says the food is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 showed that when a Jew starts the cooking and a גוי finishes it, the food is allowed. Finishing the cooking matters even more than starting it. So if the Jew did the finishing here, the food is certainly allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: a 'how much more so' argument, from a lighter case to a stronger one
its finishing; the completing of the cooking

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: קַל וָחוֹמֶר —
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: it is a kal vachomer:
if its finishing by a gentile is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָרוֹ בְּיַד יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן?
phrases.english: then its finishing by a Jew, is it not all the more so?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: קַל וָחוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2 by reasoning from the ruling in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Permitted, by a קל וחומר from the case where the גוי finished the cooking.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן agrees: forbidden only if the gentile did it all
steps.stepSummary: A statement from רבי יוחנן supports this answer. Either kind of mix (גוי places and Jew turns, or Jew places and גוי turns) is permitted. Food is forbidden only when the גוי did both the beginning and the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן (and some say it was רב אחא בר בר חנה in the name of רבי יוחנן): whether a gentile placed it and a Jew turned it, or a Jew placed it and a gentile turned it, it is permitted. It is forbidden only when both its beginning and its end were done by a gentile.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement from רבי יוחנן that backs up רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer and gives a clear general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן covers both mixed cases at once and says both are permitted. He also states the general rule: בישולי גוים is forbidden only when a גוי cooked it from start to finish. Any real part a Jew plays in the cooking makes the food permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: it was also stated (a supporting teaching)

steps.whatToRemember: The rule is that cooked food is forbidden as בישולי גוים only if a גוי did all of the cooking, from beginning to end.

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said that Rabbi Yochanan said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר בַּר חָנָה
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Acha bar bar Chana who said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
whether a gentile placed it and a Jew turned it over,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין שֶׁהִנִּיחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהָפַךְ גּוֹי — מוּתָּר,
phrases.english: or a Jew placed it and a gentile turned it over, it is permitted,
and it is not forbidden unless
its beginning and its end were done by a gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer with a statement in the name of רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: That food is permitted when a גוי placed it and a Jew turned it over.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's statement, passed on by רבה בר בר חנה (or רב אחא בר בר חנה).

steps.title: The הלכה for bread: any part by a Jew makes it permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules on bread the same way. If a גוי lit the oven and a Jew baked, or a Jew lit and a גוי baked, the bread is permitted. Even if the גוי did both, it is permitted if a Jew came and stoked the coals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said, the הלכה is: bread that a gentile lit the oven for and a Jew baked, or that a Jew lit the oven for and a gentile baked, or even that a gentile lit and a gentile baked, but a Jew came and stirred up the coals, is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the final הלכה and applies the same idea to bread baked by a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same rule from cooking applies to baking bread: it is forbidden only if a גוי did all of it. The third case is the biggest step. Even a small act, like a Jew stirring the coals so the fire burns hotter, counts as a Jewish part in the baking and makes the bread permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: stirred up or stoked the coals
it is fine; it is permitted

steps.whatToRemember: Cooked food is permitted if a Jew placed it on the fire or turned it over. Bread is permitted if a Jew lit the oven, baked it, or even only stoked the coals.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that in the third case the גוי did everything. Both the lighting and the baking were done by a גוי, but the Jew's stoking of the coals is enough to permit the bread.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical source for the common practice of a Jew stoking or adding to the fire so that bread baked by a גוי is permitted.

phrases.english: Ravina said: the halacha is:

phrases.aramaic: הָא רִיפְתָּא דִּשְׁגַר גּוֹי וַאֲפָה יִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: this bread, where a gentile lit the oven and a Jew baked,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי שְׁגַר יִשְׂרָאֵל וַאֲפָה גּוֹי,
phrases.english: or else a Jew lit it and a gentile baked,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי שְׁגַר גּוֹי וַאֲפָה גּוֹי
phrases.english: or else a gentile lit it and a gentile baked
and a Jew came and stirred up the coals in it,
it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא, הִלְכְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוחנן's rule to bread and stretches it to the act of stoking coals.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Bread is permitted if a Jew lit the oven, did the baking, or even only stoked the coals.

steps.title: Salted fish and roasted eggs: who permits and who forbids
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings two disputes. On salted fish, חזקיה permits and רבי יוחנן forbids. On a roasted egg, בר קפרא permits and רבי יוחנן forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: Salted fish made by a גוי: חזקיה allows it, and רבי יוחנן forbids it. A roasted egg made by a גוי: בר קפרא allows it, and רבי יוחנן forbids it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to two new foods and asks if a גוי's preparation makes them forbidden as בישולי גויים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These cases are less clear than ordinary cooking. Salting is not real cooking, and a roasted egg is a very simple food. Each case has one Sage who permits it, while רבי יוחנן forbids both.

phrases.english: Salted fish: Hizkiyya permits it,
phrases.notes: This means fish salted by a גוי.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yochanan forbids it.
A roasted egg: bar Kappara permits it,
and Rabbi Yochanan forbids it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּג מָלִיחַ — חִזְקִיָּה שָׁרֵי, וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָסַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from mixed גוי/Jew cooking to new kinds of food: salted fish and roasted eggs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חזקיה permits salted fish and בר קפרא permits roasted eggs. רבי יוחנן forbids both.

steps.title: רב דימי's version: both Sages permit both foods
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports the dispute differently. חזקיה and בר קפרא both permit both foods, and רבי יוחנן forbids both.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל, he said: for both salted fish and roasted eggs, חזקיה and בר קפרא permit them, and רבי יוחנן forbids them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי brings a slightly different report of the same disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, each lenient Sage spoke about only one food. In רב דימי's version, both lenient Sages permit both foods. So רבי יוחנן now stands alone against two Sages on each food, and the next story builds on this.

keyTerms.meaning: When רב דימי came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
Both this one and that one

steps.whyThisMatters: Because of this version, the lenient side now has two Sages against רבי יוחנן. The next step relies on this.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד דָּג מָלִיחַ וְאֶחָד בֵּיצָה צְלוּיָה —
phrases.english: Both salted fish and a roasted egg:
Hizkiyya and bar Kappara permit them,
and Rabbi Yochanan forbids them.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second report of the same dispute, with both lenient Sages ruling on both foods.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two Sages, חזקיה and בר קפרא, permit both foods. רבי יוחנן forbids both.

steps.title: The question at the house of ריש גלותא
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא פרוואה visits the house of ריש גלותא, and the people there ask him if a roasted egg made by a גוי is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא from Parva came to the house of ריש גלותא. They said to him: What is the law about a roasted egg?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story. Someone asks a practical question about a roasted egg made by a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the dispute stops being theory and becomes a real question about what to eat. The question sets up the ruling in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The head of the Jews in exile (in בבל)

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya of Parva
came to the house of the Exilarch.
They said to him: A roasted egg, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: בֵּיצָה צְלוּיָה מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the dispute from רב דימי's version in a real story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the law about a roasted egg made by a גוי?

steps.title: Two Sages outweigh one, so the egg is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא answers that two Sages permit and one forbids, and one opinion does not stand against two. So the egg is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: חזקיה and בר קפרא permit it, and רבי יוחנן forbids it. The words of one Sage do not stand against the words of two.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא rules leniently by following the majority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses רב דימי's version, where two Sages permit. Since the majority usually decides the law, רבי יוחנן's strict view loses.

keyTerms.term: אֵין דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹם שְׁנַיִם
keyTerms.meaning: One person's opinion does not stand against two

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: חִזְקִיָּה וּבַר קַפָּרָא שָׁרוּ,
phrases.english: He said to them: Hizkiyya and bar Kappara permit it,
and Rabbi Yochanan forbids it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹם שְׁנַיִם.
phrases.english: and the words of one do not stand where there are two.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: חִזְקִיָּה וּבַר קַפָּרָא שָׁרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The roasted egg is permitted, because two Sages outweigh רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: רב זביד: the law follows רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד tells them not to listen, because אביי ruled like רבי יוחנן. They then gave רב זביד a cup of vinegar, and he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said to them: Don't listen to him. This is what אביי said: the law follows רבי יוחנן. They gave him a cup of vinegar to drink, and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד rejects the lenient ruling and says the law is strict, like רבי יוחנן. The story ends with how the household reacted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the majority decides the law, but רב זביד has a tradition from אביי that here the law follows the single opinion of רבי יוחנן. So a roasted egg made by a גוי is forbidden. The story ends sadly: the household, unhappy with his strictness, gave him vinegar, and he died.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the majority always wins. Here אביי's tradition is that the law follows רבי יוחנן, even though he stands alone.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical law: a roasted egg made by a גוי is forbidden, like רבי יוחנן.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב זְבִיד: לָא תְּצִיתוּ לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Zevid said to them: Do not listen to him,
for this is what Abaye said:
The law follows Rabbi Yochanan.
They gave him a cup of vinegar to drink,
phrases.notes: The "him" here is רב זביד, the one who ruled strictly.

phrases.english: and he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב זְבִיד: לָא תְּצִיתוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חייא's majority ruling from step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole lenient ruling about the roasted egg.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: There is a tradition from אביי that the law follows רבי יוחנן, so the majority rule does not apply here.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A roasted egg made by a גוי is forbidden, like רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists which foods of גויים are allowed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא permits capers, leeks, מטליא, hot water, and roasted grains of גויים. It forbids a roasted egg, and it says רבי יהודה הנשיא and his בית דין voted to permit oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: capers, leeks, מטליא, hot water, and roasted grains of גויים are allowed. A roasted egg is forbidden. As for oil, רבי יהודה הנשיא and his בית דין voted on it and permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a list of foods and says which are allowed and which are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Several simple foods made by גויים are allowed. A roasted egg is forbidden, which matches רבי יוחנן and רב זביד's ruling. Oil was permitted by a vote of רבי יהודה הנשיא's בית דין.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: Capers, and leeks,
and matalya, and hot water, and their roasted grains are permitted,
phrases.notes: "Their" means foods belonging to גויים and cooked by them.

phrases.english: a roasted egg is forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמֶן — רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא וּבֵית דִּינוֹ
phrases.english: oil: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court
voted on it and permitted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַקַּפְרֵיסִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that lists more foods and agrees that a roasted egg is forbidden.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Capers, leeks, מטליא, hot water, and roasted grains are permitted. A roasted egg is forbidden. Oil was permitted by רבי יהודה הנשיא's בית דין.

steps.title: מטליא has other names
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that מטליא is the same food as פשליא, which is also called שיעתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: מטליא is the same as פשליא, which is the same as שיעתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains a word from the list in the last step by giving its other names. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food מטליא in the list was not familiar, so the ברייתא gives its other names. This leads straight to the question of what שיעתא is.

keyTerms.meaning: Another name for the same bean

phrases.english: It is taught: Matalya is
the same as pashalya, which is the same as shiata.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: הִיא הַמִּטַלְיָא הִיא פַּשִׂלְיָא הִיא שִׁיעֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the word מטליא from the ברייתא in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מטליא, פשליא, and שיעתא are all names for the same food.

steps.title: What is שיעתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this food called שיעתא is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is שיעתא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to identify the food. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the name שיעתא was not clear, so the גמרא asks what it is. The answer will describe where the food came from.

phrases.english: What is shiata?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שִׁיעֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the last name given in step 12.

steps.title: It came from מצרים: forty years ago or sixty?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says this food came from מצרים forty years ago. רבה בר בר חנה himself says it was sixty years ago.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It has been forty years since this food came out of מצרים. And רבה בר בר חנה himself said: It has been sixty years since this food came out of מצרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies שיעתא as a food brought over from מצרים. It then gives two numbers that seem to disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer identifies the food by its history: it is the bean that was imported from מצרים. But one statement says forty years and the other says sixty. That looks like a contradiction, and the next step settles it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
It is forty years
since this thing came out of Egypt,
phrases.notes: "This thing" is the שיעתא bean, which was brought over from מצרים.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה דִּידֵיהּ אָמַר:
phrases.english: and Rabba bar bar Chana himself said:
It is sixty years
since this thing came out of Egypt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שיעתא is the bean that was brought from מצרים, forty or sixty years earlier.

steps.title: No real dispute: each spoke in his own time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the two statements do not disagree. Each Sage counted the years up to his own time.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not disagree. One Sage spoke in his year, and the other Sage spoke in his year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the forty-versus-sixty problem from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said it when forty years had passed. רבה בר בר חנה said it later, when sixty years had passed. Both are counting from the same event, so both numbers are correct.
steps.whatToRemember: A roasted egg made by a גוי is forbidden, like רבי יוחנן. Simple foods like capers, leeks, מטליא beans, hot water, and roasted grains are allowed, and oil was permitted by רבי יהודה הנשיא's בית דין.

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
one Sage in his year, and the other Sage in his year.
phrases.notes: Each one counted up to the time he was speaking, twenty years apart.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא פְּלִיגִי — מָר בִּשְׁנֵיהּ וּמָר בִּשְׁנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the apparent contradiction between the two numbers in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different times: each statement was said in a different generation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן and רבה בר בר חנה disagree about when the bean came from מצרים.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both count from the same event. One spoke after forty years, and the other spoke twenty years later.

steps.title: How the plants for שיעתא were grown
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא describes how people grew and ate the plants called שיעתא. They sprouted seeds in clay, the plants blossomed during a trip to the bathhouse, and eating them cooled the whole body.
steps.simpleTranslation: They take parsley seeds, flax seeds and fenugreek seeds and soak them together in lukewarm water until they sprout. They fill new clay pots with water, soak red clay in them, and stick the sprouts into the clay. Then they go into the bathhouse. By the time they come out, the plants have blossomed. They eat them and feel cooled from the hair on their heads to the nails on their feet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps answering the question 'what is שיעתא?' by describing exactly how it was grown and eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 only told us when this food came from מצרים. Here the גמרא explains what it actually is: fast-sprouting seeds grown in wet clay. The point of the story is how quickly the plants grew and how cooling they were to eat after the hot bathhouse.

keyTerms.meaning: Fenugreek, a plant whose seeds sprout easily

phrases.english: They bring parsley seeds
and flax seeds and fenugreek seeds,
and soak them together in lukewarm water,
and leave it until it sprouts,
and they bring new clay pots
and fill them with water,
and soak red clay in them,
and stick them into it,
phrases.notes: He means they press the sprouted seeds into the wet clay.

phrases.english: and they go into the bathhouse;
by the time they come out, the plants have blossomed,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, some the one in square brackets; both mean 'by the time they come out.'

phrases.english: and they eat from them,
and they feel cool from the hair of their heads
to the nails of their feet.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַיְיתוּ בִּיזְרָא דְּכַרְפְּסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer to step 13 by describing how שיעתא was made.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שיעתא is a dish of fast-sprouting seeds grown in wet clay, which blossom during a bathhouse visit and are eaten to cool the body.

steps.title: רבי חנינא's reaction to the story
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports what רבי חנינא told him about this story. One version: 'just words', meaning it is not true. Another version: 'with words', meaning it was done with magic words.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: רבי חנינא told me, 'Words!' Some say he said, 'With words.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי tells us how רבי חנינא reacted to the story of the fast-growing plants, and the גמרא gives two versions of his reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plants cannot blossom in the time it takes to visit a bathhouse. In the first version רבי חנינא calls the story empty talk. In the second version he accepts it but says it worked through magic words, not nature.

keyTerms.meaning: Words; here, empty talk that is not true

steps.confusionAlert: The two versions differ by one letter. מילין says the story is false. במילין says it happened, but by magic words.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֲמַר לִי רַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Rabbi Chanina told me:
Words!
phrases.notes: He means it is just talk; plants can't really blossom that fast.

phrases.english: And some say he said: With words.
phrases.notes: In this version, the plants grew quickly because of magic words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֲמַר לִי רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the story in step 16, either calling it untrue or saying it worked by magic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חנינא either called the story untrue or said it worked through magic words.

steps.title: Date husks of גויים: large pot versus small pot
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that date husks of גויים heated in a large pot are forbidden, but heated in a small pot they are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: date husks of גויים whose water was heated in a large pot are forbidden. If they were heated in a small pot, they are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a ברייתא that makes the law of the date husks depend on the size of the pot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the pot of the גויים may have soaked up taste from non-kosher food. A large pot might have been used for such food, so the husks are forbidden. A small pot probably was not, so they are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Date husks, the leftovers after pressing dates

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Date husks of non-Jews
whose water was heated
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, some the one in square brackets; either way, the husks were heated in hot water.

phrases.english: in a large pot: forbidden;
in a small pot: permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַכּוּסְפָּן שֶׁל גּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about food of גויים, after the שיעתא discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Date husks of גויים heated in a large pot are forbidden. Heated in a small pot, they are permitted.

steps.title: What counts as a small pot?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how small a pot must be to count as a 'small pot' for this rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is a small pot?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a definition of 'small pot.' This sets up רבי ינאי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's rule depends on the size of the pot but never says where 'small' begins. Without a clear measure, nobody could apply the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And which is it? A request for a definition

phrases.english: And what is a small pot?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵיזוֹ הִיא יוֹרָה קְטַנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the definition of a term used in the ברייתא of step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The size limit of a 'small pot.'

steps.title: רבי ינאי: too small for a swallow to enter
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי defines a small pot as one too small for a swallow to get inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי said: any pot that a swallow cannot fit into.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ינאי answers the question by giving a measure: a pot too small for a swallow to fit inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Non-kosher birds and animals are usually bigger than a swallow. If a whole swallow cannot fit in the pot, it was probably not used to cook such food, so it is safe.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai said:
Any pot that a swallow
cannot enter into.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי: כֹּל שֶׁאֵין צִפּוֹר דְּרוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A small pot is one that a swallow cannot fit into.

steps.title: But maybe they cut the food into pieces
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: even if a whole bird cannot fit in the pot, the גויים might have cut it into pieces and put the pieces in.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps they cut it up and put it in!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי ינאי's definition. A small pot could still have held non-kosher food that was cut into pieces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ינאי's measure assumes the food goes in whole. Once food is sliced, it fits in almost any pot, so a pot too small for a whole swallow is not proven safe.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps; raises a possibility that weakens the claim

phrases.english: But perhaps they cut it into pieces and put it in!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא אַדְמוֹיֵי אַדְמוּהּ וְעַיְּילוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the definition given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's definition of a small pot (step 20).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Food can be sliced into pieces, so a pot too small for a whole swallow could still have cooked non-kosher food.

steps.title: Corrected measure: too small for a swallow's head
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the measure. A small pot is one so narrow that even a swallow's head cannot enter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a small pot is any pot that even a swallow's head cannot enter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and fixes רבי ינאי's measure to a much smaller size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pot too small for even a swallow's head is too small for cooking pieces of non-kosher meat. So the worry about cut-up food no longer applies.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, כֹּל שֶׁאֵין רֹאשׁ צִפּוֹר דְּרוֹר
phrases.english: Rather, any pot that a swallow's head
cannot enter into.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, כֹּל שֶׁאֵין רֹאשׁ צִפּוֹר דְּרוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 by narrowing the definition from step 20.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A pot too small for a whole swallow is small enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a pot too small for a swallow's head counts as small.

steps.title: Another ברייתא permits both pots
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a different ברייתא that permits the husks whether the pot was large or small.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: whether the pot was large or small, it is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that another ברייתא contradicts the first one. It permits even a large pot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא forbids a large pot and permits a small one. This ברייתא does not care about size at all and permits both. The two sources seem to clash.

phrases.english: But was it not taught:
Whether a large pot
or a small pot, it is permitted!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: אַחַת יוֹרָה גְּדוֹלָה וְאַחַת יוֹרָה קְטַנָּה מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a second ברייתא against the ברייתא of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא in step 18 that forbids a large pot.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא permits even a large pot, which contradicts it.

steps.title: The two ברייתות follow different views on נותן טעם לפגם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles the contradiction. The two ברייתות follow two different opinions about a forbidden taste that spoils the food (נותן טעם לפגם).
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This ברייתא follows the one who says that a forbidden substance which gives a spoiled taste is forbidden. That ברייתא follows the one who says that a forbidden substance which gives a spoiled taste is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by assigning each ברייתא to a different opinion about נותן טעם לפגם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Old taste soaked into a pot no longer improves the food; it only spoils it. If that kind of taste is still forbidden, a large pot is a problem, as in our ברייתא. If it is permitted, every pot is fine, as in the other ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; introduces an answer to a contradiction
In line with the one who says
Gives a spoiled taste: a forbidden taste that makes the food worse, not better

steps.whatToRemember: A small pot is one too small for even a swallow's head. The ברייתא that forbids a large pot holds that נותן טעם לפגם is forbidden. The ברייתא that permits both pots holds that it is permitted.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the pairing. The first ברייתא (large pot forbidden) goes with נותן טעם לפגם אסור. The second ברייתא (both pots permitted) goes with נותן טעם לפגם מותר.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the large-pot rule is not a separate law. It depends entirely on the wider debate about נותן טעם לפגם.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This one follows the one who says:
A substance that gives a spoiled taste is forbidden;
that one follows the one who says:
A substance that gives a spoiled taste is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר: נוֹתֵן טַעַם לִפְגָם אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns each source to a different opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seem to argue directly about pot size.
steps.terutzMaskana: They differ only because they follow different views on נותן טעם לפגם.

steps.title: Cooked oil of non-Jews is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that oil cooked by an ארמאי is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: Oil that was cooked by an ארמאי is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ruling from רב ששת: oil cooked by a non-Jew may not be used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת gives a ruling but no reason. This sets up the next step, where רב ספרא asks what the reason could possibly be.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
This cooked oil of an Aramean
is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about non-Jewish food, after the topic of the pot and the husks ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oil cooked by a non-Jew is forbidden.

steps.title: רב ספרא rejects every possible reason to forbid the oil
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא goes through three possible worries and shows that none of them applies to cooked oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: What should we worry about? If we worry that wine (יין נסך) was mixed in, wine ruins oil, so no one would mix them. If the worry is בישולי גוים, oil can be eaten raw. If the worry is the taste absorbed from the non-Jew's pots, that taste spoils the food, and a taste that spoils the food is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא challenges רב ששת. He lists every reason that could make the oil forbidden and knocks each one down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three possible problems: mixing with יין נסך, the rule of בישולי גוים, and taste from non-Jewish pots. Wine ruins oil, so no one mixes them. בישולי גוים only applies to foods that need cooking, and oil is eaten raw. The pot's old taste is נותן טעם לפגם, which is permitted. So there is no reason left to forbid the oil.

keyTerms.meaning: Food cooked by non-Jews, forbidden by the חכמים
Eaten as it is, raw. Such food is not included in בישולי גוים
Non-Jewish pots that need purging because they absorbed forbidden taste
A forbidden taste that makes the food worse, which is permitted

steps.whyThisMatters: This step shows the three main reasons non-Jewish cooked food can be forbidden. The same checklist is useful for many other foods.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
For what should we be concerned about it?
If it is because of mixing,
phrases.notes: He means mixing in wine that was used for עבודה זרה.

phrases.english: it ruins it,
if it is because of the cooking of non-Jews,
it is eaten as it is, raw,
if it is because of non-Jews' vessels that need purging,
it gives a spoiling taste, and it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא לְמַאי נֵיחוּשׁ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב ששת's ruling by showing it has no reason behind it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that cooked oil of non-Jews is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every known reason for forbidding non-Jewish food fails here: wine ruins oil, oil is eaten raw, and the pot's taste is לפגם.

steps.title: The question about boiled dates, narrowed down
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי is asked about dates boiled by non-Jews. The גמרא explains that the question is only about medium dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רבי אסי: What is the law of dates boiled by a non-Jew? Don't ask about sweet dates, because they are surely permitted. Don't ask about bitter dates, because they are surely forbidden. The question is about the in-between dates. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A question is brought to רבי אסי about boiled dates. The גמרא then narrows it down to the one kind of date that is really unclear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sweet dates can be eaten raw, so cooking them does not create בישולי גוים. Bitter dates need cooking to be eaten, so they fall under the rule. Medium dates are in between, and that is the real doubt.

phrases.english: They asked Rabbi Asi:
These boiled dates of an Aramean, what is the law?
Sweet ones, do not ask,
because they are certainly permitted.
Bitter ones, do not ask,
because they are certainly forbidden.
When you should ask is about the middle ones. What is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the idea from step 26 (food eaten raw is not בישולי גוים) to ask about dates.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Are medium-flavored dates boiled by a non-Jew permitted or forbidden?

steps.title: רבי אסי answers: my teacher Levi forbade them
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי says the question is already settled, because his teacher, לוי, forbade such dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said to them: Why are you asking? My teacher forbade them. And who was his teacher? לוי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אסי answers that medium dates are forbidden, based on what his teacher ruled. The גמרא then tells us that the teacher was לוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not come from logic. It comes from a ruling that רבי אסי received from his teacher. Medium dates are treated like bitter dates, so they are forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: My teacher (here, not רבי יהודה הנשיא)

steps.confusionAlert: Usually 'רבי' alone means רבי יהודה הנשיא. Here it means 'my teacher', and the גמרא says that teacher was לוי.

phrases.english: He said to them: What is your question?
My teacher forbade them.
phrases.notes: "רבי" here means his own teacher, not רבי יהודה הנשיא. The next line says who that was.

phrases.english: And who is he? Levi.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ מַאי תִּיבְּעֵי לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about medium dates.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Medium dates boiled by a non-Jew are forbidden, as לוי ruled.
steps.whatToRemember: Sweet dates are permitted, bitter dates are forbidden, and medium dates are forbidden, following לוי.

steps.title: Argument about שתיתא made by non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: רב permits שתיתא, and אבוה דשמואל and לוי forbid it.
steps.simpleTranslation: About שתיתא: רב permits it. The father of שמואל and לוי forbid it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument about a dish called שתיתא. It sets up the next steps, which explain what exactly they argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here we only hear the two sides, with no reasons. The question is whether שתיתא made by a non-Jew is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A dish made from roasted flour and honey

phrases.english: Shetita:
Rav permits it,
Shmuel's father and Levi forbid it.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁתִּיתָאה רַב שָׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case of non-Jewish food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב permits שתיתא, and אבוה דשמואל and לוי forbid it.

steps.title: First version: they argue about lentils made with water
steps.stepSummary: Everyone permits שתיתא made of wheat or barley and forbids lentils made with vinegar. The argument is about lentils made with water: do we make a גזירה because of the vinegar kind?
steps.simpleTranslation: With wheat and barley, everyone agrees it is permitted. With lentils made with vinegar, everyone agrees it is forbidden. They argue about lentils made with water. One opinion holds we make a גזירה forbidding this kind because of that kind. The other opinion holds we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly where רב and לוי disagree. It lays out the cases everyone agrees on and then the one case they argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vinegar of non-Jews is forbidden, so lentils with vinegar are forbidden. Lentils with water look like lentils with vinegar. לוי makes a גזירה so people will not confuse them. רב does not make that גזירה.

keyTerms.meaning: We make a protective rule forbidding this because of that

phrases.english: With wheat and barley,
everyone agrees that it is permitted,
with lentils of vinegar,
everyone agrees that it is forbidden.
Where they argue is lentils of water:

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר גָּזְרִינַן הָא אַטּוּ הָא,
phrases.english: one Sage holds we decree this because of that,
phrases.notes: "This" is lentils made with water, and "that" is lentils made with vinegar.

phrases.english: and one Sage holds we do not decree.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּחִיטֵּי וּשְׂעָרֵי כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דִּשְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the argument from step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument is only about lentils made with water, and it depends on whether we make a גזירה because of lentils with vinegar.

steps.title: Second version: they argue about wheat and barley
steps.stepSummary: Some say everyone forbids lentils made with water, and the argument is about wheat and barley: do we make a גזירה because of the lentil kind?
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: With lentils made with water, everyone agrees it is forbidden. They argue about wheat and barley. One opinion holds we make a גזירה forbidding this kind because of that kind. The other opinion holds we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the argument. Here the agreement and the disagreement are moved one level up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the גזירה for water-lentils is accepted by everyone. The question becomes whether to go even further and forbid wheat and barley שתיתא because of the lentil kind. לוי says yes and רב says no.
steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree on the idea: לוי makes a גזירה and רב does not. They only differ on which dish is in the argument: lentils with water, or wheat and barley.

phrases.english: And some say:
With lentils of water,
everyone agrees that it is forbidden,
where they argue is wheat and barley,

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר: גָּזְרִינַן הָא אַטּוּ הָא,
phrases.english: one Sage holds: we decree this because of that,
phrases.notes: Now "this" is wheat and barley, and "that" is the lentil dish.

phrases.english: and one Sage holds: we do not decree.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי בִּטְלָפְחֵי דְּמַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of step 30, moving the argument from water-lentils to wheat and barley.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone forbids lentils made with water. The argument is whether to make a גזירה on wheat and barley שתיתא as well.

steps.title: ברזילי sent two kinds of שתיתא to דוד
steps.stepSummary: רב brings a פסוק showing that ברזילי הגלעדי sent דוד two kinds of שתיתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: ברזילי הגלעדי sent two kinds of שתיתא to דוד, as the פסוק lists wheat, barley, flour and roasted grain, and also beans, lentils and roasted legumes.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא was just discussing שתיתא, it adds a related teaching from רב. He shows from a פסוק that שתיתא was a food already known in the time of דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the word קלי (roasted food) twice. The first קלי comes after wheat and barley, and the second after beans and lentils. So רב reads it as two kinds of שתיתא, one made of grain and one made of legumes, which are the same two kinds argued about in the steps before.

keyTerms.meaning: Barzillai from Gilad, who brought food to דוד when he fled from אבשלום
Roasted or parched grain or legumes

phrases.english: Rav said:
Two kinds of shetita
Barzillai the Gileadite sent to David,
as it is written: "Beds, and basins, and earthen vessels,
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 17:28

phrases.english: wheat, and barley, and flour, and roasted grain,
and beans, and lentils, and roasted legumes",
phrases.notes: קלי appears twice: once after the grains and once after the legumes. That gives the two kinds of שתיתא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: תְּרֵי מִינֵי שַׁתִּיתָאה שַׁדַּר בַּרְזִילַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי לְדָוִד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related teaching about the same food, שתיתא, after the argument over whether it is allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two kinds of שתיתא, grain and legume, and both are hinted at in the פסוק about ברזילי.

steps.title: In נהרדעא everyone sells שתיתא freely
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that today שתיתא is sold by the basketful in נהרדעא, and no one follows the strict view of אבוה דשמואל and לוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And now they bring out basket after basket of it to the markets of נהרדעא, and no one worries about the ruling of אבוה דשמואל and לוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the שתיתא discussion with a report of what people actually do. In נהרדעא, non-Jews' שתיתא is sold everywhere and people buy it without worry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Back in step 29, אבוה דשמואל and לוי forbade שתיתא while רב permitted it. This line shows that common practice follows the lenient view, even in נהרדעא, the home city of שמואל and his father.

keyTerms.meaning: נהרדעא, a major Jewish city in Babylonia, home of שמואל

steps.whatToRemember: In practice, people were lenient about non-Jews' שתיתא and did not follow the strict view of אבוה דשמואל and לוי.

phrases.english: And now they bring it out
basket after basket to the markets of Nehardea,
and there is no one who is concerned
about that ruling of Shmuel's father and Levi.
phrases.notes: This points back to their view that שתיתא is forbidden (step 29).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשְׁתָּא הוּא דְּקָא מַפְּקִי צַנֵּי צַנֵּי לְשׁוּקֵי דִּנְהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up the שתיתא topic by describing actual practice.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Practice follows the lenient view: שתיתא from non-Jews is openly sold and eaten.

steps.title: חזקיה: if wine is known to be inside, even benefit is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about כבשין, and חזקיה limits it: the משנה allows הנאה only when wine is usually added, but if we know wine was added, even הנאה is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: pickled foods whose usual way is to have wine put in them. חזקיה said: The משנה only taught this (that הנאה is allowed) when it is just their usual way. But when we know for sure that wine is in them, even הנאה is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, about non-Jews' pickled foods that usually have wine added. חזקיה explains that the משנה's permission for הנאה only applies when we are unsure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה forbids eating such pickles but allows benefiting from them, for example by selling them. חזקיה says this is because we are only guessing that wine is inside. If we know wine was added, the יין נסך makes the food forbidden even for הנאה.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose usual way is (to have wine added)
Where it is known for sure
Benefit, such as selling or other use, as opposed to eating

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two levels. Eating is forbidden in both cases. The argument is only about הנאה (benefit) when we know for sure that wine was added.

phrases.english: "And pickled foods whose usual way is to put wine in them."
phrases.notes: This is a quote from our משנה, which forbids eating these but allows benefit.

phrases.english: Hizkiya said:
They only taught this where it is just their usual way,
but where it is known for sure,
it is forbidden even for benefit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁדַּרְכָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next line of the משנה, about כבשין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pickled foods that only usually have wine are forbidden to eat but allowed for הנאה. If wine is known to be inside, they are forbidden even for הנאה.

steps.title: Why is this different from fish brine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges חזקיה: the רבנן allowed הנאה from מורייס even though it has wine, so why should known-wine pickles be forbidden for הנאה?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different from מורייס, which the רבנן allowed for benefit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges חזקיה's strict rule by comparing it to another case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מורייס is a fish brine that has wine mixed in, and the רבנן still allowed people to benefit from it. If wine inside does not forbid הנאה there, why should it forbid הנאה in pickled foods?

keyTerms.meaning: A fish brine or sauce that non-Jews sometimes mixed with wine
What is different? (asks why two cases are treated differently)

phrases.english: And what is different from fish brine,
which the Rabbis permitted for benefit?
phrases.notes: The רבנן here are the ones who disagree with רבי מאיר about מורייס.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מִמּוּרְיָיס דְּשָׁרוּ רַבָּנַן בַּהֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges חזקיה's ruling in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's ruling that pickles known to contain wine are forbidden even for הנאה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מורייס also contains wine, yet the רבנן allow הנאה from it. The two cases seem the same.

steps.title: Wine for smell versus wine for taste
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in מורייס the wine only removes the bad smell, but in pickles it is added to give a sweet taste.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the wine is added to take away the bad smell. Here, it is added to sweeten the taste.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends חזקיה by showing that the two cases are really different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In fish brine, the wine just covers the fishy smell and is not really part of the flavor. In pickles, the wine is there to give the food its taste, so it counts much more as part of the food. That is why it can forbid even הנאה.

phrases.english: There, the wine is to remove the bad smell;
phrases.notes: "There" is the fish brine.

phrases.english: here, it is to sweeten the taste.
phrases.notes: "Here" is the pickled foods.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם — לְעַבּוֹרֵי זוּהֲמָא, הָכָא — לְמַתּוֹקֵי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine mixed into any food has the same effect, so מורייס and pickles should be treated alike.
steps.terutzMaskana: The purpose of the wine matters. Wine that only removes a smell is less important than wine that gives flavor, so known-wine pickles are forbidden for הנאה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It introduces the idea that the job the forbidden wine does in a food can change how strict the law is.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even when known, benefit is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees with חזקיה and says that even when we know wine was added, הנאה is still permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even when it is known for sure that wine is inside, it is also permitted for benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second opinion that argues with חזקיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוחנן, it makes no difference whether we are guessing or know for sure. In both cases eating is forbidden but הנאה is allowed. This sets up a new question that the גמרא asks right away.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Even where it is known for sure, it is also permitted,
phrases.notes: Permitted for benefit only. Eating is still forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ בְּיָדוּעַ נָמֵי מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opinion that disagrees with חזקיה in step 34.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pickled foods of non-Jews are permitted for הנאה even when it is known that wine was added.

steps.title: Why is this different from רבי מאיר's fish brine ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן: רבי מאיר forbids הנאה from מורייס, so why should pickles known to contain wine be permitted for הנאה?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different from מורייס according to רבי מאיר, who forbids it even for benefit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's lenient view. The answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that מורייס, which has wine mixed in, is forbidden even for הנאה. רבי יוחנן says pickles are permitted for הנאה even when we know wine is inside. So the גמרא asks how, in רבי מאיר's view, wine could forbid הנאה in fish brine but not in pickles.

phrases.english: And what is different from fish brine according to Rabbi Meir,
who forbids it even for benefit?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מִמּוּרְיָיס לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר דַּאֲסִיר בַּהֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 37, using the opposite side of the מורייס argument from step 35.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that pickles known to contain wine are permitted for הנאה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי מאיר forbids הנאה from מורייס because of the wine in it, pickles known to contain wine should also be forbidden for הנאה.
